items.body:
### Environment

Node version: v24.15.0
npm version:  11.12.1
Local ESLint version: v10.4.0
Global ESLint version: 
Operating System: Windows 11 (NT 10.0.26200)


### What parser are you using?

Default (Espree)

### What did you do?

I ran the `no-unused-vars` rule on some code where I had an unused function declaration. When I used my editor's quick-fix to apply the `removeVar` suggestion on that function,it produced syntactically invalid JavaScript because it didn't account for ASI (Automatic Semicolon Insertion). 

Here's the minimal setup to see it happen:

<details>
<summary>Configuration</summary>

```js
{
  rules: { "no-unused-vars": "error" }
}

```


</details>

```js
const x = 1
function unused() {}
(a) => {}
```


### What did you expect to happen?

The `removeVar` suggestion should either produce syntactically valid JavaScript, or not be offered when removing the declaration would create an ASI hazard.


### What actually happened?

Applying the `removeVar` suggestion produced syntactically invalid JavaScript:

```js
const x = 1

(a) => {}
```

Without a semicolon after `const x = 1`, the parser interprets `1(a)` as a call expression on the numeric literal `1`, then hits `=>` and fails:

```
Unexpected token =>
```

The issue appears to originate from the FunctionDeclaration and ClassDeclaration removal paths in handleFixes, which call fixer.removeRange(parent.range) directly and do not appear to perform the ASI-safety checks used for VariableDeclarator removals

### Link to Minimal Reproducible Example

https://eslint.org/play/#eyJ0ZXh0IjoiY29uc3QgeCA9IDFcbmZ1bmN0aW9uIHVudXNlZCgpIHt9XG4oYSkgPT4ge31cbiIsIm9wdGlvbnMiOnsicnVsZXMiOnsibm8tdW51c2VkLXZhcnMiOlsiZXJyb3IiXX0sImxhbmd1YWdlT3B0aW9ucyI6eyJwYXJzZXJPcHRpb25zIjp7ImVjbWFGZWF0dXJlcyI6e319fX19

### Participation

- [x] I am willing to submit a pull request for this issue.

### AI acknowledgment

- [ ] I did not use AI to generate this issue report.
- [x] (If the above is not checked) I have reviewed the AI-generated content before submitting.

### Additional comments

Also affects `ClassDeclaration`:

```js
const x = 1
class Unused {}
(a) => {}
```

Applying the `removeVar` suggestion produces the same invalid output and parser error.

For comparison, in an ASI-sensitive variable-declaration scenario, ESLint still reports the unused variable but suppresses the removal suggestion. This suggests that variable removals already have protection against unsafe declaration removal, while function and class removals do not.

To reproduce the issue, apply the removeVar suggestion for unused.

labels.name: accepted

items.body:
### Environment

- ESLint version: `v10.4.0`
- Node.js version: `v24.15.0`
- npm version: `11.12.1`
- Operating System: Windows 11 

### What parser are you using?

Default (Espree)

### What did you do?

Running `--fix` on an async function callback that has a multi-line block comment between `function` and the parameter list (`repro.js`):

```js
foo(async function /*
*/ () { return 1; });
```

Config:

```json
{ "rules": { "prefer-arrow-callback": ["error"] } }
```

Command (local clone at commit `9067f9492`):



### What did you expect to happen?

The autofix should give back valid JavaScript. If it can't do that safely (like in this case), it should skip the fix and just report the warning instead.

### What actually happened?



The autofix turned `repro.js` into this:

```js
foo(async  /*
*/ () => { return 1; });
```

This is broken — it doesn't parse anymore. The ESLint homepage says "ESLint fixes are syntax-aware so you won't experience errors introduced by traditional find-and-replace algorithms." but that's exactly what happened here.

The failure shows up in two ways:

**1. ESLint itself reports a parse error on the same `--fix` run (exit code 1):**

```
repro.js
  2:7  error  Parsing error: Unexpected token =>

✖ 1 problem (1 error, 0 warnings)
```

**2. Espree also chokes on the post-fix file:**

```bash
node -e "require('espree').parse(require('fs').readFileSync('repro.js','utf8'),{ecmaVersion:'latest',sourceType:'module'})"
```

```
SyntaxError: Unexpected token => (2:7)
```

perfectly valid JS to something that can't even be parsed.






### Link to Minimal Reproducible Example

https://eslint.org/play/#eyJ0ZXh0IjoiZm9vKGFzeW5jIGZ1bmN0aW9uIC8qXG4qLyAoKSB7IHJldHVybiAxOyB9KTsiLCJvcHRpb25zIjp7InJ1bGVzIjp7InByZWZlci1hcnJvdy1jYWxsYmFjayI6WyJlcnJvciJdfSwibGFuZ3VhZ2VPcHRpb25zIjp7InBhcnNlck9wdGlvbnMiOnsiZWNtYUZlYXR1cmVzIjp7fX19fX0=

### Participation

- [x] I am willing to submit a pull request for this issue.

### AI acknowledgment

- [ ] I did not use AI to generate this issue report.
- [x] (If the above is not checked) I have reviewed the AI-generated content before submitting.

### Additional comments

**Why the post-fix output is invalid (spec reference)**

The `AsyncArrowFunction` production in the spec says:

> `async [no LineTerminator here] AsyncArrowBindingIdentifier [no LineTerminator here] => AsyncConciseBody`

The `CoverCallExpressionAndAsyncArrowHead` variant has the same `[no LineTerminator here]` between `async` and the arrow head. A block comment that has `\n` in it counts as a LineTerminator for this rule. In the fixed output, the comment `/* \n */` sits between `async` and `()`, so it puts a line break where one isn't allowed.

Spec link: https://tc39.es/ecma262/#prod-AsyncArrowFunction

### Environment

Node version:  v24.15.0
npm version: 11.12.1
Local ESLint version: v10.4.0
Global ESLint version:
Operating System: windows


### What parser are you using?

Default (Espree)

### What did you do?

I found a false positive in ESLint's `no-constant-condition` rule.

## Minimal reproduction

**Configuration:**
```json
{
  "rules": {
    "no-constant-condition": ["error", { "checkLoops": "all" }]
  }
}
```

**Code:**
```js
async function foo() {
    while (true) {
        await bar();
    }
}
```


### What did you expect to happen?

**Expected:** No ESLint error should be reported for the `while (true)` condition.

**my reasoning**
 The loop body contains `await`, which suspends execution and allows external code to run. This is semantically identical to `YieldExpression` in generators—both allow the loop condition to potentially change between iterations. The rule already correctly handles `YieldExpression` by clearing the loop tracking set, so `AwaitExpression` should be handled identically.


### What actually happened?

**Actual:** ESLint reports:
```
Unexpected constant condition.
```

on line 2 (`while (true)`), even though the loop body contains `await` that could cause the condition to change.


### Link to Minimal Reproducible Example

https://eslint.org/play/#eyJ0ZXh0IjoiYXN5bmMgZnVuY3Rpb24gZm9vKCkge1xuICAgIHdoaWxlICh0cnVlKSB7XG4gICAgICAgIGF3YWl0IGJhcigpO1xuICAgIH1cbn1cbiIsIm9wdGlvbnMiOnsicnVsZXMiOnsibm8tY29uc3RhbnQtY29uZGl0aW9uIjpbImVycm9yIix7ImNoZWNrTG9vcHMiOiJhbGwifV19LCJsYW5ndWFnZU9wdGlvbnMiOnsicGFyc2VyT3B0aW9ucyI6eyJlY21hRmVhdHVyZXMiOnt9fX19fQ==

### Participation

- [x] I am willing to submit a pull request for this issue.

### AI acknowledgment

- [ ] I did not use AI to generate this issue report.
- [x] (If the above is not checked) I have reviewed the AI-generated content before submitting.

### Additional comments

I think this is a clear asymmetry between two semantically equivalent control-flow suspension mechanisms (`yield` and `await`), and the fix mirrors the already-accepted pattern for `YieldExpression`.

The rule handles `YieldExpression` [here](https://github.com/eslint/eslint/blob/main/lib/rules/no-constant-condition.js#L174) but has no corresponding `AwaitExpression` handler.

items.body:
### Environment

Node version: v22.x
npm version: 10.x
Local ESLint version: latest (main)
Global ESLint version: N/A
Operating System: Windows 11


### What parser are you using?

Default (Espree)

### What did you do?

<summary>Configuration</summary>

```js
/* eslint for-direction: "error" */
// Case 1: counter moves in wrong direction inside a SequenceExpression
for (let i = 10; i < 20; i--, j++) {}

// Case 2: should NOT report — net effect on counter is +1 (valid loop)
for (let i = 10; i < 20; i--, i += 2) {}

// Case 3: counter modified twice, opposite directions — net effect is 0
for (let i = 10; i < 20; i--, i++) {}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

1. Case 1 → error: The update clause in this loop moves the variable in the wrong direction.
2. Case 2 → No error (net effect on i is +1, loop terminates normally)
3. Case 3 → No error / direction unknown (counter modified twice with opposing directions; net effect is statically ambiguous)


### What actually happened?

No output for any of the three cases. The rule passes silently without reporting an error.



### Link to Minimal Reproducible Example

https://eslint.org/play/#eyJ0ZXh0IjoiLyogZXNsaW50IGZvci1kaXJlY3Rpb246IFwiZXJyb3JcIiAqL1xuXG5mb3IgKGxldCBpID0gMTA7IGkgPCAyMDsgaS0tLCBqKyspIHt9Iiwib3B0aW9ucyI6eyJydWxlcyI6eyJmb3ItZGlyZWN0aW9uIjpbImVycm9yIl19LCJsYW5ndWFnZU9wdGlvbnMiOnsicGFyc2VyT3B0aW9ucyI6eyJlY21hRmVhdHVyZXMiOnt9fX19fQ==

### Participation

- [x] I am willing to submit a pull request for this issue.

### AI acknowledgment

- [ ] I did not use AI to generate this issue report.
- [x] (If the above is not checked) I have reviewed the AI-generated content before submitting.

### Additional comments

The tricky part is handling cases where the counter appears more than once in the sequence:

for(i = 10; i < 20; i--, i++) — net effect is 0 → infinite loop, but statically ambiguous
for(i = 10; i < 20; i--, i += 2) — net effect is +1 → valid loop, must NOT report
Proposed safe behavior: If the counter appears in more than one expression within the sequence, treat direction as unknown and skip. Only report when exactly one expression in the sequence modifies the counter in the wrong direction.

I am willing to submit a pull request for this issue (PR #20701 has a working implementation pending team review of the edge cases above).
